# Getting started with AWS {.unnumbered} This lab will cover creating AWS users, groups, attaching policies, creating access keys, and configuring the AWS command line interface (CLI). ## AWS set up First, you'll need to log into AWS. This is separate from your regular Amazon account, and comes with different tiers. I highly recommend turning on the MFA and using something like the [Microsoft Authenticator app](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/mobile-authenticator-app) to login. When you first access AWS, your landing page will look something like this: ![AWS Console](img/lab7-aws-console.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} This is your **AWS Console**, where you'll launch new instances, select storage devices, containers, etc. In the first part of this lab I'll cover Identity and Access Management (IAM) in the Console, and in the second part we'll install and configure the AWS CLI. ## Identity and Access Management (IAM) Back in the **AWS Console**, we need to create a group, attach policies to this group, then create user. ### Creating Groups In the **AWS Console**, we'll navigate to: **IAM** \> **IAM User groups** \> **Create group** ![Look for IAMin 'Recently visited'](img/lab7-aws-console-iam.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"} ![Select 'IAM user groups'](img/lab7-aws-create-group.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} Give the group a meaningful name: `dev-deploy-group` Under **Attach permissions policies**, search and select the following: * `AmazonEC2FullAccess` * `AmazonS3FullAccess` Down the road, we should replace these with scoped custom policies later, but for now it will get us up and running. Click **Create Group** and you should see something like: ![](img/lab7-aws-group-created.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} As we can see, this group doesn't have any users, so we'll create and add them next. ### Creating Users Back in **AWS Console**, we'll navigate to: **IAM Users** \> **Create User** ![](img/lab7-aws-iam-create-user.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} We'll give the user a meaningful username: `mjfrigaard-cli` ![Create IAM user](img/lab7-iam-user-details.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} We have the option to check "*Provide user access to the AWS Management Console*". Right now `mjfrigaard-cli` only needs the CLI, so we'll leave it unchecked and give the user only the access it uses. A user without a Console password can't sign in to the Console, so there's one less credential to protect. We can turn Console access on later without recreating the user (see [Console access for `mjfrigaard-cli`](#console-access)). Now, under **Add user to group**, we select `dev-deploy-group` and click **Next** ![Add user to group](img/lab7-iam-add-user-to-group.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} At this point, we're given a chance to review our selections before confirming, which is also a great opportunity to quickly cover AWS IAM users and groups. ![Review user/group selections](img/lab7-iam-review-user-group.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} ### IAM: Core concepts AWS IAM is somewhat like like Linux users and groups, but instead of file permissions, IAM uses *policies* to control who can do what, and where. Three core concepts to know about AWS IAM: 1. A **`user`** is an identity (a person or a service).[^iam-users] 2. A **`group`** is a collection of `users` that share permissions.[^iam-groups] 3. A **`policy`** is a JSON document that says what actions are allowed on what resources[^iam-policies] [^iam-users]: Read more about [AWS IAM users](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_users.html) [^iam-groups]: Read more about [AWS IAM user groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups.html) [^iam-policies]: Read more about [AWS IAM policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html) Users don't get permissions directly, they inherit permissions from the groups they belong to. If you've worked with Linux groups and file permissions before, the table below might be helpful for mapping the AWS IAM concepts. | AWS IAM concept | Linux user/groups analog | |----------------------------------|--------------------------------------| | IAM User | User | | IAM Group | Group | | IAM Policy (JSON file) | File permissions (`rwx`) | | IAM Users list | `/etc/passwd` | | Elevated permissions granted by attached policy | `sudo` | | Access vis access key ID + secret access key | SSH keys | So far, we've created/logged into our AWS account, then from the **AWS Console**, we 1) created an IAM group, 2) attached IAM policies to the IAM group, 3) created an IAM user, and 4) assigned that user to the IAM group. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘IAM users, groups and policies’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph TD AWS(["AWS
Account"]) --"create"--> Groups("IAM Groups") AWS --"create"--> Users("IAM Users") Policy[/"IAM Policies"/] Policy --"attach"--> Groups Groups --"inherit"--> Users style Policy fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style AWS fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Groups fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Users fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff ``` #### Policies determine permissions For example, say we have a new developer, Alice (`alice`). Alice wouldn't get any permissions herself, but she'd be a member of the `devs` group, which has a `S3ReadWrite` policy attached, which allows Alice access to the `my-data` bucket. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘Policies and permissions’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph LR Policy[/"Policy:
S3ReadWrite"/] Groups("IAM Group:
devs") Users("IAM User:
alice") Resource[("S3 Bucket:
my-data")] Policy --> Groups --> Users --> Resource style Policy fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Resource fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Groups fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Users fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff ``` A policy is like a permissions file that specifies and **effect** (allow or deny), an **action** (what operation, like `s3:PutObject`), and the **resource** (what it applies to, i.e., a specific bucket).[^start-aws-1] [^start-aws-1]: This is conceptually similar to a Linux ACL entry, but scoped to AWS API actions instead of filesystem operations. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘Policy effects, actions, and resources’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph LR Policy[/"Policy
Document"/] --> Effect("Effect:
Allow") Policy --> Action("Action:
s3:PutObject") Policy --> Resource[("Resource:
arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*")] style Policy fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Effect fill:#3E2A1E,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Action fill:#3E2A1E,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Resource fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff ``` #### What about multiple groups? Like a Linux user being in multiple groups (`sudo`, `docker`, `www-data`), an IAM user can belong to multiple IAM groups. Consider the user `alice` below: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘Multiple IAM groups’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph TD Users(["alice"]) --"In Group"--> DevGroup("devs") Users --"In Group"--> OpsGroup("ops") DevGroup --> S3Policy[/"Policy:
S3 Access"/] OpsGroup --> EC2Policy[/"Policy:
EC2 Access"/] S3Policy --> S3[("S3
Buckets")] EC2Policy --> EC2["EC2
Instances"] style Users fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:center,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style DevGroup fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:center,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style OpsGroup fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:center,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style S3Policy fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style EC2Policy fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style S3 fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style EC2 fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff ``` Alice ends up with the *combined* permissions of both `devs` and `ops` groups (just like a Linux user inheriting from multiple group memberships). #### Identities In AWS, identities can be *human users* (i.e., people like `alice` logging in via console or CLI). But identities can also be *service/automation users*, which are things like GitHub Actions or applications that need programmatic access (like a system account or a service account key). ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘Humans and services’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph TD AWS(["AWS
Account"]) --"IAM User
(human)"--> Human("alice") AWS --"IAM User
(service)"--> Service("gha-bot") Human --> ConsoleAccess["Console Login +
CLI Keys"] Service --> Keys["Access Keys Only,
No Console"] style AWS fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Human fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:center,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style Service fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:center,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style ConsoleAccess fill:#3E2A1E,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Keys fill:#3E2A1E,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff ``` ### IAM: Recap Below is a full picture of IAM users, groups, policies and resources. We'll be using all of these to stand up an EC2 instance, put our `vetiver` model/data into an S3 bucket, and give GitHub Actions the S3 credentials. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘Humans and services’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph TD AWS(["AWS
Account"]) AWS --> Users("IAM Users") AWS --> Groups("IAM Groups") AWS --> Policies[/"IAM Policies"/] AWS --> Roles["IAM Roles
(optional, for cross
service access)"] Users --> Groups Groups --> Policies Roles --> Policies Policies --> Resources["AWS Resources:
S3, EC2, etc"] style AWS fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Policies fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Roles fill:#3E2A1E,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Groups fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Users fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Resources fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff ``` [**IAM Roles**](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html) (not covered in depth here) are like temporary identities services assume, e.g., an EC2 instance assuming a role to access S3 without needing stored credentials at all. This is the more secure long-term pattern, but access keys are the simpler starting point. ## Creating Access Keys In the **IAM users** dashboard, we can see: 1) the `dev-deploy-group`,\ 2) the policies we attached to this group (`AmazonEC2FullAccess` and `AmazonS3FullAccess`), and\ 3) the new user we just created (`mjfrigaard-cli`) In the **Summary** section, there is an option to **Create access key**: ![IAM users dashboard](img/lab7-iam-user-dashboard.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} We want to click on **Create access key** under the **Security credentials tab**. The **Use case** we want is the **Command Line Interface (CLI)**: ![](img/lab7-aws-cli-access-key.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"} Follow the steps in the documentation (be sure to store the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key pair somewhere safe!). Next we'll cover installing the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI) on our local machine. This will allow us to control AWS from the command line. ## Install AWS CLI First we run the standard `apt update`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo apt update ``` ::: Next we download the latest version via the official installer: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o "awscliv2.zip" ``` ::: Install an `unzip` utility: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo apt install unzip -y ``` ::: Use `unzip` on the downloaded `awscliv2.zip` file: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} unzip awscliv2.zip ``` ::: Finally, we install `aws`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo ./aws/install ``` ::: You should see: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} # You can now run: /usr/local/bin/aws --version ``` ::: ::: ### Verify install ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws --version ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} # aws-cli/2.35.15 Python/3.14.5 Linux/7.0.11-76070011-generic exe/x86_64.pop.24 ``` ::: ::: ## Logging in Use the `aws login` command to log in with the Terminal: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws login ``` ::: Select a region by clicking Enter: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} No AWS region has been configured. The AWS region is the geographic location of your AWS resources. If you have used AWS before and already have resources in your account, specify which region they were created in. If you have not created resources in your account before, you can pick the region closest to you: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-infrastructure/latest/regions/aws-regions.html. You are able to change the region in the CLI at any time with the command "aws configure set region NEW_REGION". AWS Region [us-east-1]: ``` ::: Then the browser opened and I was able to log in as the `root` user: ![Browser confirmation](img/lab7-aws-cli-login-success.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"} I logged in as `root` here because it's the only identity with Console access so far (we skipped Console access when we created `mjfrigaard-cli`). The `root` user has unrestricted access to the entire account, so going forward I recommend using the `mjfrigaard-cli` IAM user and saving `root` for the few tasks that require it. Signing in as `mjfrigaard-cli` needs a Console password, which we add in [Console access for `mjfrigaard-cli`](#console-access). We'll configure the access keys for `mjfrigaard-cli` in the CLI Configuration section below. :::: {.callout-warning collapse='true' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [Alternatives recommended]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} You might see the following recommendation for logging in: ![](img/lab7-login-cli-recommendation.png){width='100%' fig-align='center'} I used the `aws login` command from the Terminal, but still needed an Access Key ID and Secret Access Key to configure the `dev-deploy` profile. ::: :::: ### AWS Terminology Review We've just created a new group, user, access key ID, *and* secret access key. Lets review these before going forward, because it got confusing for me the first time I completed this lab. #### 1. What is an ARN? **ARN** = Amazon Resource Name. You may have noticed this under the **Summary** section for the `mjfrigaard-cli` user: ![](img/lab7-aws-user-arn.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"} The ARN a unique identifier for a specific AWS resource (a user, bucket, instance, policy, etc).[^start-aws-2] ARNs are similar to fully qualified file paths, but for AWS resources. [^start-aws-2]: Read more about AWS ARN's in the [official documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference-arns.html). This is how it works: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:user/mjfrigaard-cli ``` ::: | Part | Value | Meaning | |---------------------|--------------|------------------------------------| | `arn` | arn | Fixed prefix | | `aws` | aws | Partition (the standard AWS, not something like GovCloud or China) | | `iam` | iam | Service | | (blank) | none | Region (IAM is global, so it doesn't specify a region) | | `ACCOUNT_ID` | Account ID | Which AWS account owns this user | | `user/mjfrigaard-cli` | Resource | this is an IAM **user** named `mjfrigaard-cli` | ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) uniquely identify AWS resources’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph LR ARN["ARN"] --"Partition"--> Partition("aws") ARN --"Service"--> Service("iam
s3
ec2") ARN --"Region"--> Region("us-east-1 ") ARN --"Account ID"--> Account("ACCOUNT_ID") ARN --"Resource Path"--> Resource("user/mjfrigaard-cli") style ARN fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style Partition fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style Region fill:#3E2A1E,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style Service fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style Account fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff style Resource fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff ``` In plain English: *"IAM user named `mjfrigaard-cli` in AWS account `ACCOUNT_ID`."* **Should I keep my ARN a secret?** No--ARNs are not credentials. They are identifiers, similar to a username or a URL. It's safe to share, log, or put in documentation. It does not grant access by itself (they just identify a resource). However, you should keep the Access Key ID + Secret Access Key secret, because these are used to authenticate. #### 2. IAM Account IDs/Aliases By default, our AWS account is identified with a 12-digit number (called an Account ID). An Account ID is not secret like access keys (alone it can't grant access to anything), but don't share it unnecessarily. You may have seen the option to log in with an IAM account alias instead. An account alias is a human-readable name you can set to work in place of the Account ID. To create an account alias, use the following command: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws iam create-account-alias --account-alias my-company-name ``` ::: This changes your console log in URL from: ```{.default} https://ACCOUNT_ID.signin.aws.amazon.com/console ``` to: ```{.default} https://my-company-name.signin.aws.amazon.com/console ``` This is a purely cosmetic change; it doesn't affect permissions or ARNs. ## CLI Configuration Back in the Terminal, we're going to configure a `dev-deploy` profile with the access keys for the IAM user in `dev-deploy-group`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws configure --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: This will prompt you for: 1. Access Key ID 2. Secret Access Key 3. Region (`us-east-1`) 4. Output format (`json`) The commands above only create a named credential profile stored locally at the following location (nothing was sent to AWS yet): ```{.default} ~/.aws/credentials (keys) ~/.aws/config (region/output format) ``` We can test our configuration with: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws sts get-caller-identity --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: This asks AWS: *"Using these credentials, who am I?"* It returns the following: ``` json { "UserId": "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "Account": "NUMBER_SET", "Arn": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:user/mjfrigaard-cli" } ``` AWS's security token service (STS) validated our keys and returned: * `UserId`: unique internal ID for this IAM user * `Account`: AWS account number * `Arn`: confirms we are authenticated as `mjfrigaard-cli` ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: ‘Humans and services’ %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph LR CLI(["CLI
(stored keys)"]) STS("get-caller-identity") CLI --"Security
Token
Service"--> STS STS --Returns--> Response("UserId
Account
Arn") style CLI fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style STS fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#fff style Response fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,font-size:14px,text-align:left,font-family:monospace,color:#ffffff ``` This is the standard way to confirm our CLI credentials are valid and check which identity they belong to. ## Console access for `mjfrigaard-cli` {#console-access} When we created `mjfrigaard-cli`, we skipped Console access because the user only needed the CLI. That changes once `aws login` or the Console asks for an IAM user sign in. The IAM user screen asks for an account ID or alias, an IAM username, and a password, and `mjfrigaard-cli` doesn't have a password yet. ![The **IAM user sign in** screen asks for an account ID or alias, an IAM username, and a password](img/lab7-aws-iam-user-login.png){width="50%" fig-align="center"} When we log into the **Console** as `root`, we can see the **IAM users** dashboard shows this. ![The **IAM users** dashboard: `mjfrigaard-cli` has no password age and Console access is **Disabled**](img/lab7-aws-iam-users-dashboard.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} The **Password age** column for `mjfrigaard-cli` is empty (`-`) and **Console access** is **Disabled**, which means the user has never had a Console password. There's nothing to reset, so we enable Console access instead. Sign in to the Console as `root` one last time and: 1. Go to **IAM** \> **IAM users** and click `mjfrigaard-cli`. 2. Open the **Security credentials** tab. 3. Under **Console sign-in**, click **Enable console access**. ![Enable console access on the **Security credentials** tab](img/start-aws-console-sign-in.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} 4. Choose **Custom password** and enter a strong password. Leave "*User must create a new password at next sign-in*" unchecked, because this is our own account. ![Choose **Custom password** in the **Enable console access** dialog](img/start-aws-console-sign-in-pw.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"} 5. Click **Enable console access**. The confirmation shows the Console sign-in URL with the account ID or alias. ![The **Console password** confirmation shows the sign-in URL, user name, and a one-time view of the password](img/start-aws-console-password.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"} From here on, sign in as the IAM user with the account ID or alias, `mjfrigaard-cli`, and the new password. Save `root` for the few tasks that require it: billing, changing the `root` email or password, closing the account, or restoring access if every IAM admin is locked out. ![Console Home signed in as `mjfrigaard-cli`: the account menu shows the IAM user, and widgets outside its permissions show **Access denied**](img/start-aws-console-home-cli.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} ## Rotating access keys The access key we created for `mjfrigaard-cli` is a long-term credential. It never expires on its own, so anyone who finds it can use it until we delete it. The **IAM users** dashboard shows the key's age in the **Active key age** column, and it flags keys older than 90 days with a warning icon. Rotating means replacing the key with a new one on a schedule. An IAM user can hold two access keys at once, which lets us rotate without downtime. We create the new key, switch everything over, and only then retire the old one. ### Checking the current keys Start by listing the user's keys and checking when each one was last used. These commands need IAM permissions. We attach `IAMFullAccess` to `dev-deploy-group` in [Stand up an EC2 instance](aws-ec2.qmd), and after that the `dev-deploy` profile can run them: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws iam list-access-keys \ --user-name mjfrigaard-cli \ --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws iam get-access-key-last-used \ --access-key-id OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID \ --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: `list-access-keys` returns each key's ID, status, and creation date. `get-access-key-last-used` returns the last date, service, and region the key was used. A key that hasn't been used in months can be deleted without rotating. ### Rotating the key The rotation takes five steps, and the old key keeps working until the fourth: 1. Create a second key. Copy the secret from the output; AWS won't show it again. ```bash aws iam create-access-key \ --user-name mjfrigaard-cli \ --profile dev-deploy ``` 2. Put the new key everywhere the old one lives. For this book that's only the local `dev-deploy` profile. GitHub Actions doesn't use this key ([GitHub Actions and S3](gha-s3.qmd) uses a role instead), so there's nothing to update there. ```bash aws configure --profile dev-deploy ``` 3. Confirm the new key works: ```bash aws sts get-caller-identity --profile dev-deploy ``` 4. Deactivate the old key. A deactivated key can be turned back on if something still depended on it. ```bash aws iam update-access-key \ --user-name mjfrigaard-cli \ --access-key-id OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID \ --status Inactive \ --profile dev-deploy ``` 5. After a few days with nothing broken, delete it: ```bash aws iam delete-access-key \ --user-name mjfrigaard-cli \ --access-key-id OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID \ --profile dev-deploy ``` ### Rotation best practices The five steps above work for any long-term key, but I've found the order matters more than the commands. Each step leaves a way back until the old key is gone. The diagram below shows the full cycle, including what to do when something breaks: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Access key rotation cycle' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph TD Start(["Key reaches 90 days"]) Create("Create a
second key") Update("Update every place
the old key lives") Works{"New key
works?"} Deact("Deactivate
the old key") Broken{"Anything break

A calendar reminder works better than waiting for the warning icon. * Keep one active key: the second slot is for rotation, not for a spare. Two active keys means two secrets to protect. * List where the key lives before you start: for this book it's only `~/.aws/credentials`. A key you forgot to update is the most common reason a rotation breaks something. * Verify before you deactivate: `aws sts get-caller-identity` should return the `mjfrigaard-cli` ARN with the new key. If it doesn't, the old key still works, so nothing is lost. * Deactivate before you delete: a deactivated key can be turned back on, but a deleted key is gone for good. #### Cleaning up the old key Before deleting the old key, check that nothing used it after we deactivated it. An inactive key can't sign requests, so its last used date should stay the same: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws iam get-access-key-last-used \ --access-key-id OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID \ --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: Copies of the old key can also outlive it in notes, scripts, or shell history. Search for the old key ID and remove any copies you find (`-I` skips binary files, and `-l` prints only the file names): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} grep -rIl "OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID" ~ 2>/dev/null ``` ::: #### When a key leaks A leaked key changes the order. Deactivate it right away, even if something still depends on it, then create the new key and update each place it's used. A few minutes of downtime is better than leaving a working key in someone else's hands. ### Key management practices Rotation limits how long a leaked key stays useful, but a few habits keep keys from leaking at all: * Never commit keys: they belong in `~/.aws/credentials` or a secrets store (like GitHub secrets), never in code, `.env` files under version control, or chat messages. * Delete unused keys: `get-access-key-last-used` shows which ones are safe to remove. * Prefer short-lived credentials where you can: `aws login` and IAM Identity Center issue credentials that expire on their own. GitHub Actions can assume an IAM role through OpenID Connect (OIDC) instead of storing keys at all (we set this up in [GitHub Actions and S3](gha-s3.qmd)). ## Recap 1. We created the `dev-deploy-group` IAM group, attached the `AmazonEC2FullAccess` and `AmazonS3FullAccess` policies, and added the `mjfrigaard-cli` user to it. The user has no permissions of its own; it inherits them from the group. 2. We created an access key for `mjfrigaard-cli` with the Command Line Interface (CLI) use case. The Access Key ID and Secret Access Key authenticate requests, so they stay private (ARNs, by contrast, are identifiers and safe to share). 3. We installed the AWS CLI with the official installer, confirmed it with `aws --version`, and stored the keys in a `dev-deploy` profile with `aws configure`. Running `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile dev-deploy` returned the `mjfrigaard-cli` ARN, which confirms the credentials work. 4. We enabled Console access for `mjfrigaard-cli`, so everyday sign ins use the IAM user instead of `root`. 5. We rotate the access key every 90 days by creating a second key, switching the `dev-deploy` profile to it, then deactivating and deleting the old one.
